title: Wales show they have bench impact in All Blacks win
article_text:
They say rugby is now a game that relies on 23 players.

There was ample evidence of that during Wales' remarkable 35-28 win against New Zealand last Saturday.

The headline acts were the 346 tackles made by the team, which was a world record for an international match.

The 38 tackles managed by lock Dafydd Jenkins matched the top individual tally, while Jac Morgan (31), James Botham (30), Eddie James (25), captain Dewi Lake (24) and Max Llewellyn (23) were not far behind.

It was the impact of the bench that also proved crucial in the defensive stand of the final quarter.

Replacement back rower Taine Plumtree popped up with two crucial turnovers, while Gareth Thomas and Ben Carter made a combined 32 tackles in 42 minutes.

Ospreys prop Thomas managed 19 in 26 minutes, while lock Carter's return was 13 in 16 minutes to add to the remarkable statistics and contributions.

Thomas has been Wales' third-choice loose-head in recent times behind Nicky Smith and Rhys Carre.

He found himself promoted to the bench last Saturday, with Smith starting and Carre left out of the squad.

Thomas responded by providing one of the most impressive replacement defensive displays in living memory, especially for a prop.

"I have not made as many tackles in such a short space of time," said Thomas.

"But I kept looking up and they were running at me! It was a wild last 20 minutes, but every single person on the pitch was doing their job.

"Everybody was doing what they could, emptying every little bit of energy they had to stop them from scoring."

Alongside his tackles, he also held All Blacks number eight Wallace Sititi over the line, one of three vital interventions of its kind, with Botham, Morgan and fly-half Dan Edwards also involved in the efforts that denied New Zealand.

"It was a sketchy moment because there was a lot of space there," said Thomas.

"I knew if I went to hit him hard it could have been a try, easily so I kind of soaked him up over the line.

"It's something we've been working with, a last resort that Peter Murchie and Dan Lydiate [Wales defence coaches] have brought in.

"It was nice that transfered to the game. Straight after you're thinking what's my next job and don't think about it.

"But after the game I've had that video sent to me 50 to 100 times on social media. I've watched it a few times and it's a big moment."

Thomas, 33, is one of the elder statesmen in the group.

"It's a very special feeling," said Thomas.

"I was sat in bed the other night, just watching the videos of reactions in pubs and places around Wales. I love it how it made everyone feel, what it meant to people.

"I had a message saying how special it made their 92-year-old friend and he's happy to go to the grave now after that. So special to make people feel like that.

"We can't stop watching the reactions because it makes you feel like a fan.

"I would love to have been a fan watching it, it shows what it means to see ex-players with tears in their eyes."

Dragons co-captain Carter, 25, was dropped to being a replacement following the 28-21 win against Japan, with Adam Beard coming into start alongside Jenkins.

Beard made his own telling contribution in an improved Wales line-out and racked up 21 tackles in 64 minutes before Carter came onto help finish the job.

"I probably would have liked to have spent a bit more time with the ball and maybe a bit further up the field," said Carter.

"I do enjoy the defensive aspect of the game, so it was brilliant.

"They were coming at us very direct and it always felt good in those defensive sets and we were pleased.

"I was tired and I can't imagine how the boys were feeling that they had already played 60 minutes.

"There were some big shifts and tackle numbers from a lot of the boys.

"The biggest thing was you could feel the the fight for each other on the pitch, and the supporters could see it as well."

Carter, who has played 23 internationals, hopes to be involved this weekend against Australia, while Beard is suffering from a sore shoulder.

"There's a lot of belief in this group anyway and they believe that's the sort of performance we can put in," said Carter.

"Just to live it and to get that result will only help our confidence.

"There is probably a bit of expectation on us now, and the group looks forward to carrying that into these next games."

title: The Youth Olympic medallists set for Global Youth 7s in Auckland
article_text:
Rugby Australia has unveiled the Australia Under 18 Girls and Australian Schoolgirls squads for this year’s Global Youth 7s in Auckland, with 10 medallists from the Dakar Youth Olympics set to participate in the prestigious age-grade event.

Queensland Reds prospect Aimee Henry captained Australia at the Youth Olympics, with the talented squad making it through to the gold medal match. But the Aussies fell just short of gold in an extra-time thriller against Kenya, who claimed a 17-12 win in the Senegal capital.

Henry and nine other sevens representatives from those Games will again get the chance to wear green and gold on the world stage, with RA naming 26 players across two squads to play across the ditch on December 18 to 20.

Dakar silver medallists Grace Buchanan, Keira Callaghan, TJ Murray, Layne Prince, Cobi Ryan-Last and Darci Turinui have been selected in the U18 Girls squad. Another three silver medallists have been named in the Australian Schoolgirls side.

90 per cent of those in the full-time Australia Sevens program played at Global Youth 7s during their rise through the ranks, including prolific try-scorers Maddison Levi and Faith Nathan, and captain Isabella Nasser.

The invitational tournament brings together future stars of the HSBC SVNS Series, with some of the world’s best emerging sevens talent taking the field. Mitch Bebb and Asako Ono will coach the U18 side, who claimed titles in 2018, 2019 and 2023.

“The Global Youth 7s is an incredibly important part of our pathway,” Rugby Australia Women’s Sevens National Talent Pathways Manager Lachlan Parkinson said.

“It provides our emerging athletes with the opportunity to experience international competition, test themselves against some of the best young talent in the world and understand what it takes to compete at the next level.

“Just as importantly, it allows us to continue building depth within Australian Rugby Sevens and creating a sustainable pathway for the next generation of athletes coming through.

“Both squads have an exciting mix of talent and potential, and we believe both teams have the ability to compete very well at this tournament.”

Australia U18 Schoolgirls Head Coach Luke Zeremes added: “This is the fourth consecutive year that an Australian Schoolgirls Rugby Sevens team has been selected, and it’s exciting to see the continued growth and development of the program.

“We have players representing New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria and Western Australia in 2026, which highlights the depth of emerging talent across the country.

“The Global Youth Sevens in Auckland is a fantastic opportunity for these young athletes to test themselves against quality international opposition, with a mix of national development programs and invitational teams from New Zealand, Australia and beyond.

“It’s an exciting tournament that will challenge the players both individually and collectively, while providing invaluable experiences and opportunities to continue their development.”

title: Black Ferns Sevens icons return in 18-player squad for SVNS Series
article_text:
Michaela Brake, Sarah Hirini and Shiray Kaka are back in black for the 2026/27 HSBC SVNS Series, with the Olympic gold medallists named in an 18-player Black Ferns Sevens squad. Coach Cory Sweeney has also selected three uncapped players in the group.

Brake, Hirini and Kaka all became first-time mothers over the last 18 months, and are now juggling having young families with the demands of elite sport. Social media sensation Kaka documented this journey with the ‘Back to Black’ series.

The experienced trio are joined in the lineup by uncapped players Kavanah Lene, Le-Oxeayn Maiu’u and Renee Holmes. Holmes starred as the Black Ferns won the postponed 2021 Rugby World Cup on home soil, and was a regular starter during last year’s event as well.

Holmes recently described Black Ferns Sevens and Black Ferns teammate Jorja Miller as “an absolute freak” in an interview with RugbyPass, after the two had shared the field in recent SVNS warm-up events both at home and abroad.

Miller, who is a two-time World Rugby Sevens Player of the Year, has retained the vice-captaincy, as confirmed by New Zealand Sevens on Tuesday. Risaleaana Pouri-Lane will continue to lead the side, taking on captaincy duties full-time last season.

Maia Davis, Jazmin Felix-Hotham, Jaymie Kolose, Danii Mafoe, Manaia Nuku, Mahina Paul, Alena Saili, Kelsey Teneti, Katelyn Vahaakolo and Olive Watherston have also been named to represent the Black Ferns Sevens this season.

“It’s been great to see the energy of the new players in the squad alongside the leadership of our more experienced core,” Sweeney said.

“It has been a very competitive preseason with players pushing for places and that’s a positive sign as we look toward the start of the HSBC SVNS Series.”

The Black Ferns Sevens dominated the SVNS Series regular season in 2025/26, winning five of six events. But the New Zealanders fell just short in the World Championship race, with arch-rivals Australia taking out titles in Valladolid and Bordeaux.

title: Olympic medallist returns to All Blacks Sevens on loan from Chiefs
article_text:
Tokyo Olympics silver medallist Andrew Knewstubb has returned to the All Blacks Sevens on loan from the Chiefs, with the Willie Rickards-coached squad also featuring a handful of uncapped players for the 2026/27 HSBC SVNS Series season.

Knewstubb has helped Canterbury win back-to-back provincial titles and is coming off a maiden Super Rugby Pacific campaign with the Highlanders. The first five-eighth recently moved up north, selected by the Chiefs in the wider training group draft.

But the Chiefs have loaned Knewstubb out to the All Blacks Sevens, just as the Hurricanes have done with Waisake Salabiau. Salabiau is one of five uncapped prospects in the 22-man squad, along with Grady Forbes, Adam Morrison, Brayden Neilson and Nathan Salmon.

Salmon is coming off a historic season with Northland, with the Taniwha ending their long-lasting Ranfurly Shield drought en route to the final. The winger also spent time Stateside with the New England Free Jacks during the 2026 Major League Rugby season.

Brothers Rob and Brady Rush are in the All Blacks Sevens fold, also looking to build on an unforgettable NPC campaign with Northland. Rob was named Player of the Match after the Shield win over Canterbury in Christchurch.

Rob Rush will help lead the side this season, with New Zealand Sevens announcing the captains on Wednesday. Rush and experienced campaigner Sione Molia have been named co-captains, while former skipper Tone Ng Shiu also brings experience to the squad.

Joe Webber has been included, with coach Willie Rickards bringing the five-time World Series [SVNS Series] champion back.

Sam Clarke, Jayden Keelan, Kele Lasaqa, Michael Manson, Ngarohi McGarvey-Black, Fletcher Morgan, Sofai Notoa-Tipo, Akuila Rokolsioa, Bradley Tocker and Riley Williams round out the group.

“Our group has come together really well through the preseason and our leaders have set a great example for the new players coming into the environment,” Rickards said.

“There’s a sense of excitement about the season and some young players who are ready to make their mark.”

The All Blacks Sevens will announce a 13-player travelling squad for the Dubai and Cape Town Sevens on Friday, November 20.

title: Natasha Hunt on PWR, Gloucester-Hartpury upheaval and the Lions: ‘It would be the cherry on top of the cake’
article_text:

Returning from Red Roses camp to prepare for a new Premiership Women’s Rugby (PWR) season, Natasha ‘Mo’ Hunt was hit by the realisation of how much had changed. For the first time in three campaigns, Gloucester-Hartpury enter not as defending champions but as challengers; Saracens, the league’s first dynastic power, were restored to their throne in June with a final demolition job against the upstart Trailfinders. A relinquishing of their crown precipitated a summer of drastic change – gone from an environment known colloquially known as “The Circus” are, among others, Zoe Stratford, Tatyana Heard, Sarah Beckett, Sisilia Tuipulotu, Bethan Lewis and Kelsey Jones.

Or, as ringmaster Hunt puts it: “Pretty much my friendship group has all gone.” New mother Stratford (nee Aldcroft) was her business partner and co-captain; having lost charismatic coach Sean Lynn to Wales last year, there is certainly a different feel about the place.

“Personally, it does feel like a huge change,” Hunt admits. “It will take some getting used to. I’m so unbelievably chuffed for Zo in her next chapter, but I’m gutted that I don’t get to pull on the shirt again with her in the changing room. She is an unbelievable athlete and human to be around.”

But out of upheaval can come opportunity. The outstanding France centre Gabrielle Vernier is an eye-catching arrival in the West Country, and Hunt is confident she and her squad can retain a unique culture built around the person as much as the player. “You get the best out of people when you know what makes them tick and on a deeper level,” she explains. “That’s something we’ve driven at Gloucester.

“It’s not something we’ve ever spent loads and loads of time on. It needs to be organic to have a good culture. We were really pro on recruiting good people. If someone was to come in, they had to be a good human and add to the environment. The forward pack I had in front of me was just insane for three years, but it was also about the humans they were off the pitch. It is about enjoying your time together. With the Red Roses and Gloucester-Hartpury, I’ve been lucky that I’ve been part of two teams with that unbelievable culture and unbelievable athletes who are really driven to push. Have high standards, but also be a bit silly with each other.”

Those high standards met new challenges in a fascinating season last time around. Though Gloucester-Hartpury topped the table, their semi-final defeat to Trailfinders came as little surprise given how things had coalesced in Ealing during the course of the campaign. If few would have forecast Bristol as eight-placed finishers, the Bears finished with just one win fewer than the beaten finalists – and have brought in Ellie Kildunne to supercharge their revival following a somewhat messy exit from Harlequins.

A reshaping of the league perhaps looms with Irish, Welsh and Scottish interest in fielding teams in the future, and the Rugby Football Union (RFU) courting American investment, but, for now, the scramble for play-off places could be more competitive than ever. Tighthead prop Tuipulotu has pitched up at Quins, where she is joined by Marlie Packer and Rosie Galligan – two more new parents after the pair welcomed a daughter in October.

Stratford – once back from maternity leave – Heard and Beckett could turn Sale Sharks into contenders; Loughborough have added a Canadian core; and even Leicester, of which there were real concerns last year, have lured Wallaroos whizz-kid Caitlyn Halse to Welford Road. And that’s without mentioning Exeter, with a squad as complete as any.

There may be an added significance to this season, too. The first Women’s British and Irish Lions squad will be named in mid-May just before the PWR season resumes following the Six Nations; with virtually all of those hoping to figure in Jo Yapp’s selection plying their trade in England, and club contests sometimes offering a better gauge than at Test level given the Red Roses’ dominance, the battle for places could be fierce.

“I’ve been lucky enough to be involved in two Team GB squads, and having all of those different cultures is great,” Hunt says. “If anyone says they aren’t thinking about it, they are lying, because it is such a huge opportunity as individuals but for the women’s game as well. I hate talking about it. What will be will be. The only thing that I can control is how I play.”

It is more than 15 years now since the scrum half made her international debut. For a player who contemplated retirement after her omission from England’s World Cup squad in 2022, the Lions is a pretty significant carrot for keeping going – and a dedicated character, who gave up alcohol for a year before the Red Roses’ triumph on home soil, has a drive to get there.

“Sometimes people get stuck into your age but I want to flip the narrative on it. I’m 37 now and that should be celebrated. I was capped in 2011; I’ve been doing this a hell of a long time now.

“I want to go out still on the top of my game. If you can still perform to the level required, I don’t think age should ever be a consideration when picking someone. [The Lions] is a reason for still playing. It was part of the decision-making to keep going and see if that is something I could potentially achieve. But at the same time, I’m so content with my career. It won’t define me and my rugby. It would just be the cherry on top of the cake.”

title: The PGA Tour is simplifying, but rules governance remains complicated
article_text:
The most powerful word Brian Rolapp, the CEO of the PGA Tour, used late Monday afternoon while talking to reporters in a remote press conference was simple. Well, two longer forms of it, more precisely: simplify and simplification. The occasion was the announcement of the concluding work, conducted over the past 18 months, by the Tour’s Future Competition Committee, chaired by Tiger Woods, who was not present for this confab powered by . . . Microsoft Teams, the preferred video conferencing service of the PGA Tour.

“We have seen the success of PGA Tour University across the PGA Tour system and it will now serve as the basis of eligibility on the Korn Ferry Tour,” Rolapp said at the start, reading from prepared remarks. “From the outset, we said we wanted to simplify the model and ensure there was a clear path for top performers at every stage of their career.”

I’m drawn to the word, because the world is complicated and golf is simple, or it should be. What is golf but an ancient overland game requiring its players to bat a small ball toward and into an annoyingly small hole with specified equipment, playing, all the while, your ball as it lies, the first and most essential rule that coexists with various others?

The play conducted by PGA Tour players is essentially simple. It aggregates the adventures of a group of men who are “chasing a little white ball” (per Rory McIlroy, repeatedly). The players count strokes. They count their own shots played, while counting the shots played by others, too. A two-way check. (Can you imagine tax returns if any of us could audit anybody we wished?) In theory, any and all golfers, male or female or otherwise, can play their way onto the PGA Tour. All you have to do is shoot the scores. In a manner of speaking and in a far more specific context, Rolapp was saying that very thing. He was summarizing the work of the Future Competition Committee.

“Before I open up to questions, I will briefly address LIV because I suspect it might come up today. We have heard from our fans and we know that they want the best players playing together and we share that view. I have said that from day one when I took the job I am interested in doing whatever makes the PGA Tour better. That said, as we have a membership organization, we have rules, and as I shared before, they exist to ensure fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter and they will be enforced.”

Any competition committee at any level can run with that sentence.

I used to play in a fall golf event where you couldn’t make more than a triple bogey on any hole. It was a rule, a generous one, you could say, aimed at speeding up the pace of play for the field while keeping hope alive for individual players.

The LPGA recently announced new rules for 2027 aimed at improving the pace of play. When it’s your turn, you have to play your shot within 60 seconds. The clock is ticking. Six seconds too long will cost you a shot. Sixteen seconds too long will cost you two. Rules matter and they will be enforced. You can only hope that is a statement that applies across the game, wherever it is played.

The rules that govern play on the PGA Tour are not decided by its Future Competition Committee. But all golf competitions, including this week’s event at Sea Island, in the Georgia Lowcountry and hosted by a local, Davis Love III, start with its rules. One of the greatest insights I ever got about how to view the role of the rules in golf came from Davis, years ago. We were talking about how TV viewers could call in possible rules violations they observed. “It’s not like you’re trying to get away with anything,” Love said, “so why wouldn’t you want all the help you can to turn in the most accurate scorecard possible?” Flawless logic.

The first page of the rulebook instructs golfers to play the course as you find it and to play your ball as it lies. Bryson DeChambeau was penalized at the British Open at Royal Birkdale this year because he didn’t do that. In a manner of speaking, a viewer picked up on that: a rules official watching on TV. The official saw DeChambeau taking heavy-footed steps in the rough behind his ball in the rough of the fifth hole in the second round, thereby improving his lie. I couldn’t see it, watching the TV replays, but people with far more experience than I, including Rory McIlroy watching in real time, could. The Open’s competition committee gave DeChambeau two shots. He had failed to play his ball from its original lie.

Earlier this month, McIlroy received a two-shot penalty in the first round of the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, a DP World Tour event, for violating the same rule in a different way. On the 12th hole, with the flange of his sand wedge, he pressed too firmly into the grass behind his ball. The rule permits you to press “lightly,” letting a player rest the club with its actual weight but not apply his or her own force. In layman’s terms, you can’t shove your clubhead behind the ball.

In my casual golf, I almost never see anybody violate this rule, in spirit or in fact. Jack Nicklaus never did, because he always hovered his club over the ball when it was in a grassy lie. Watching a replay of the McIlroy situation, I could not readily see an issue. A rules official, watching on TV, could — or eventually could. A small tuft of grass that had been immediately behind McIlroy’s ball no longer was. He had changed his lie by being too aggressive while preparing to play his shot.

title: Olympic Solidarity support helps rugby sevens teams make history at Dakar 2026
article_text:
The first Olympic sporting event to be held on African soil provided a memorable stage for rugby sevens, with developing rugby nations making their mark and young athletes showcasing the growing strength of the game across the continent.

Among the standout achievements were Kenya's historic gold medal in the women's competition and Madagascar's bronze, with both teams having participated in an Olympic Solidarity-supported training camp in Tunisia just weeks before stepping onto the podium in Dakar.

Organised by World Rugby in October in collaboration with the International Olympic Committee, the camp provided an important opportunity for both teams to fine-tune their preparations ahead of the Youth Olympic Games, combining on-field training with educational sessions covering anti-doping, safeguarding and the Olympic values.

The initiative reflected the wider objectives of Olympic Solidarity, which supports athletes and National Olympic Committees around the world, helping to strengthen sporting development and create opportunities for young athletes to compete on the international stage.

For Kenya and Madagascar, that support formed part of a journey that culminated in unforgettable moments in Dakar. Kenya's Rising Lionesses claimed gold in dramatic fashion, defeating Australia 17-12 in extra time, with Mitchelle Chemtai scoring the decisive try to secure the country's first Olympic rugby sevens gold medal. The victory also marked the first time an African nation had won rugby sevens gold at either the Olympic Games or Youth Olympic Games.

Madagascar, meanwhile, celebrated a milestone of its own, defeating Czechia 26-10 to secure bronze and claim the nation's first-ever Olympic medal in any sport.

Reflecting on Kenya's achievement, Kenya Rugby Union CEO Thomas Odundo highlighted the importance of the support received throughout the team's development. “I'm very proud of the girls. What started as developing the national sports system was then followed by this training camp and finally materialised into a medal. That's just amazing.”

The success of both teams underlined the importance of sustained investment in emerging rugby nations, with initiatives such as the Olympic Solidarity-supported camp helping to provide young athletes with the preparation, knowledge and experience needed to perform at the highest level.

World Rugby CEO Alan Gilpin, who attended the Games in Dakar, witnessed the historic achievements and the enthusiasm surrounding rugby sevens at Africa's first Youth Olympic Games. “Dakar 2026 was a special moment for rugby and for the growth of the game in Africa. Seeing Kenya and Madagascar make history on the Olympic stage was incredibly inspiring and demonstrated the talent and potential that exists across the continent.

“Through our collaboration with Olympic Solidarity, we can help provide young players and emerging rugby nations with opportunities to develop, prepare and compete. The achievements in Dakar are a wonderful example of what that support can help make possible, and we look forward to building on this momentum.”

The rugby sevens competition produced memorable performances across both tournaments, with France securing men's gold ahead of South Africa and Argentina, while Kenya topped the women's podium ahead of Australia and Madagascar.

Beyond the medals, Dakar 2026 demonstrated the opportunities that rugby sevens can create for young athletes around the world, and the important role that collaboration and targeted development initiatives can play in helping more countries realise their potential on the Olympic stage.

title: Smashing Stats: Hong Kong Open 2026
article_text:
Xie Xingfang, the last women's singles player to win consecutive editions, celebrates her second title in 2007.

With the final HSBC BWF World Tour Finals 2026 spots on the line, LI-NING Hong Kong Open 2026 plays a decisive role in this season’s conclusion.

Here are the key numbers and storylines to watch as the tournament marks its final year as a Super 500 event.

Top seeds Wang Zhi Yi, Yuki Fukushima and Feng Yan Zhe/Huang Dong Ping have all tasted past success in Hong Kong.

Wang and Feng/Huang are two of the three defending champions returning, alongside fellow Chinese stars Liang Wei Keng/Wang Chang.

Glory for second seed Wang will make her the first women’s singles player since Tai Tzu Ying in 2017 to win consecutive editions.

She could also emulate Xie Xingfang, the last Chinese to win the category twice in a row in 2007.

Fukushima, now partnering Mayu Matsumoto, won in 2018 with Sayaka Hirota.

Japan boast three seeded pairs in women’s doubles this time as they look to end a drought in the category stretching back to Fukushima and Hirota’s triumph.

Men’s singles second seed Kunlavut Vitidsarn aims to expand Thailand’s winners list by replicating their solitary victory in 2001 via Sujitra Ekmongkolpaisarn in women’s singles.

Indonesia are yet to produce a champion in women’s singles, in which they possess sixth seed Putri Kusuma Wardani.

Wardani has an added incentive this year – winning the title could mean qualification to the World Tour Finals.

Likewise, Koki Watanabe could achieve both – for self and country – if he triumphs in men’s singles.

Men’s singles has featured remarkable parity, with players representing six different flags topping the podium across the last six editions.

Malaysia, who havenot had success in men’s doubles since 1999 (Cheah Soon Kit/Yap Kim Hock), count on eighth seeds Man Wei Chong/Tee Kai Wun and Aaron Tai/Yap Roy King.

China are the sole nation to celebrate podium toppers at the last four Hong Kong Opens.

Standout Stat: Since 2011, Chinese mixed pairs have won eight of the 12 editions – a 66.7 per cent strike rate that stands as the joint-highest across all five categories during that span.

title: Campari Group makes football sponsorship debut with Aperol-UEFA EURO 2028 partnership
article_text:
Campari Group is entering the international football sponsorship landscape through a landmark partnership between its Aperol brand and UEFA, becoming the official spritz partner of UEFA EURO 2028 and the European Qualifiers.

The agreement marks Campari Group’s first-ever partnership with UEFA and its first major international football sponsorship. The collaboration provides Aperol with a platform to strengthen its global brand presence by associating with one of European football’s premier sporting events.

The partnership will extend across the European Qualifiers and the UEFA EURO 2028 final tournament, giving Aperol visibility throughout the competition cycle. The tournament will be hosted across England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland, with 24 national teams competing in 51 matches.

As part of the agreement, Aperol will develop consumer engagement initiatives and brand activations around the competition, centred on shared celebrations and social experiences. The association also reflects the brand’s Italian aperitivo heritage and its positioning around bringing people together.

Simon Hunt, CEO of Campari Group, said, “This partnership brings to life our purpose of unlocking human connections on a global stage that unites millions of fans. As our first major international football partnership and first-ever sponsorship with UEFA, UEFA EURO 2028 gives Aperol an exceptional opportunity to engage audiences at scale and support the brand’s ambition to expand its presence across our new formats and opening up new occasions.”

Guy-Laurent Epstein, UEFA Executive Director of Marketing, added, “We are delighted to partner with Campari Group and welcome their iconic brand Aperol as an official sponsor of UEFA EURO 2028 and the European Qualifiers. UEFA EURO is much more than a football tournament; it is a celebration that brings people together through unforgettable shared experiences. Aperol’s longstanding ability to create moments of connection and conviviality makes it a natural fit for our events, and we look forward to working together to create a memorable tournament.”

The agreement comes as Campari Group looks to accelerate Aperol’s international expansion. The company highlighted the brand’s growth from approximately 60 million Aperol Spritz servings annually two decades ago to around 1.5 billion today. It is also extending the brand’s portfolio through formats such as Aperol Spritz On Tap, Ready to Serve and Ready to Drink.

For Campari Group, the UEFA partnership represents an opportunity to leverage football’s international reach to broaden consumer engagement and create new occasions for brand consumption.

title: Analyst predicts Walmart as surprise buyer for sports media rights in 2027
article_text:
The sports media rights marketplace is preparing for a shakeup.

As the decade nears its end and the NFL almost certainly exits its current set of media rights deals, networks and streamers are preparing for what could be a monumental shift in the industry. Legacy broadcasters continue to consolidate or get spun off from their corporate parents, while streaming giants continue to battle each other for engagement. The NFL is the 3,000-pound gorilla in the room that will dictate how networks and streamers approach other media rights opportunities in the next several years.

Major properties that will be on the market before or during NFL negotiations include the 2030 FIFA World Cup (set to be awarded by the end of 2026), MLB, NHL, and Premier League (all of which expire in 2028), Big Ten and PGA Tour (2030), and NASCAR (2031).

The usual suspects will kick the tires on some or all of these. ESPN, Skydance (CBS/TNT), Fox, NBC/Peacock, Prime Video, Netflix, Apple, YouTube, Versant, The CW, Ion, and DAZN will all be in the mix. But one company that might come out of left field is Walmart, according to Bank of America Securities analyst Jessica Reif Ehrlich, who floated the retailer as a potential bidder for live sports in 2027.

Ehrlich revealed her prediction at a Sports Business Journal conference on Tuesday, which reportedly drew “intrigued murmurs from the audience.”

Walmart would be an unconventional bidder, to say the least. It does not own a major streaming service, nor any broadcast or cable networks. Walmart does, however, own Vizio, a television brand it acquired for $2.3 billion in December 2024. Since the acquisition, Vizio has risen to the third most popular television brand in America, behind Samsung and LG.

Walmart’s acquisition focused on scaling its advertising and media businesses. Each Vizio television set comes preloaded with its own smart TV interface and the WatchFree+ app, a Vizio-owned FAST platform that features over 400 live and local channels and a vast library of movies and shows.

Should Walmart enter the sports-rights market, its strategy could be similar to Roku’s, which is seen as one of Vizio’s primary competitors in the space. Roku has acquired some smaller, more affordable packages like Sunday morning MLB games (2024-2025) users onto its FAST platform, The Roku Channel.

It seems unlikely that Walmart would get in the mix for a major rights package, though the company is certainly capitalized enough to do so if it wanted.

title: Anytime Fitness Australia Named Official Gym Partner of West Coast Eagles
article_text:
Anytime Fitness Australia has signed a two-year commercial agreement to become the Official Gym Partner of the West Coast Eagles, spanning both the club’s Australian Football League (AFL) and AFL Women’s (AFLW) programmes.

The partnership connects the national fitness franchise network, comprising more than 647 clubs and 800,000 members nationwide, directly with the Eagles’ record-breaking supporter base of 115,324 financial members across Western Australia.

By linking Anytime Fitness’s club footprint across Greater Perth, the Peel region, and regional Western Australia with the Eagles’ elite men’s and women’s squads, the deal aims to bridge high-performance sport with everyday community health.

The agreement follows Anytime Fitness’s recent major activation in Perth as the Official Gym Partner of ExPRO, Australia’s fitness, wellness, and lifestyle festival, further consolidating the brand’s commercial and recruitment expansion along the Western Australian coastline.

Anytime Fitness Australia Managing Director, Simon Thompson, highlighted the value of aligning with Western Australia’s largest sporting institution to drive grassroots fitness participation.

“The West Coast Eagles unite generations of West Australians, with a loyalty and pride that reaches far beyond the football field.”

“Our ambition is to give more people across WA a welcoming place to train, build strength and feel their best.

“Becoming the Official Gym Partner of the Eagles’ AFL and AFLW teams builds on that commitment, bringing together two organisations that share a passion for sport, fitness and the positive role they play in people’s lives,” Thompson said.

West Coast Eagles CEO, Don Pyke, underscored the natural synergy between elite athletic performance and accessible community wellbeing.

“We’re proud to welcome Anytime Fitness to the West Coast Eagles and look forward to building a strong partnership across our AFL and AFLW programs.”

“Both organisations understand the important role sport and physical activity can play in bringing people together and supporting their health and wellbeing.

“We’re excited to work together to encourage more people in our community to get active and enjoy the benefits of an active lifestyle,” Pyke said.

title: Iran war dents Middle East sports model as events are canceled or postponed. F1 bucks the trend
article_text:
Two season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events. This includes two Formula 1 races earlier this year in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain.

The conflict has upended the region's image as a safe haven where governments and sponsors have kicked in billions to lure mega-sports events. This comes as Europe and North America appear wary of such lavish spending.

“The situation could change but the geography will not change,” Sebastian Sons, who follows sports in the Middle East with the German research institute CARPO, told The Associated Press. “The Middle East and the Gulf region are always a volatile and fragile region.”

Going ahead is an endorsement for doing business in the region, but has also prompted concerns about safety from some teams and staff. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of auto racing's world governing body FIA, has said “we are fully prepared” to pull off the two races: Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6.

Ben Sulayem is from the United Arab Emirates.

A MotoGP race was held in Qatar on Nov. 8 on the track where F1 races. MotoGP is operated by Liberty Media, which also runs F1.

“Holding the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi signals that those two are stable and able to host large-scale sporting events. It is important they are seen to be open for business,” Kristian Ulrichsen, a political scientist at Rice University's Baker Institute, told The AP.

“Predictability in long-term decision-making and policy planning,” Ulrichsen added, “made the region so attractive as a host of mega-events at a time when many cities and countries around the world are rethinking the cost of doing so.”

Qatar’s reputation is on the line. It held the 2022 World Cup and is a co-favorite — with India — to land the 2036 Olympics. It’s also host next year to the basketball World Cup (Aug. 27-Sept. 12) and has the 2030 Asian Games.

It took a hit last week when the United States pulled its team from the boys’ under-17 World Cup being played in Qatar.

Saudi Arabia and its Persian Gulf neighbors have spent big to hold major sports events but were cutting back on mega-sports funding before the war began nine months ago.

“For Saudi, the war has accelerated the need to find economies, to maybe reassess what was feasible and what wasn’t,” Ulrichsen said. He said landing the “big prize,” two years ago — the 2034 World Cup — probably honed Saudi's focus.

“Qatar and the UAE will probably have to at some point do the same,” he added.

Major events called off, postponed or relocated include the two Formula 1 races earlier in the season, and the WTA season-ending tennis finals and soccer’s monthlong Asian Cup — both originally scheduled for Saudi Arabia. The 2027 Dakar Rally was also moved from Saudi Arabia to Portugal and Morocco.

The region has been using sports to promote “soft power” to enhance its brand. But Saudi Arabia now faces hard power with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels having struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport in Riyadh. Riyadh’s business district has also recently been targeted.

The war has also affected the large Gulf air carriers and changed travel patterns in the region.

“One of the things Iran did during the war was to deliberately attack the connective tissue between Gulf states and the world,” Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told The AP. “This includes ports, airports, hotels and data centers — signaling that Iran can attack important issues beyond hydrocarbons and challenge the Gulf states’ ambitions to diversify.”

Sons, the researcher at the German think tank, estimated that Saudi Arabia invested more than $6 billion in international sports between 2021 and 2023. Sons said the country hosted more than 100 international sports events between 2019 and 2024.

A visible failure was the bankruptcy of LIV Golf, which reports say was funded by approximately $5 billion from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Saudi Arabia also canceled the 2029 Asian Winter Games, planned for the Trojena ski village in the south of the desert kingdom.

The event has been moved to Almaty, Kazakhstan, which lost to Beijing in a close vote for the 2022 Winter Olympics.

Ulrichsen said Saudi Arabia was backing off what seemed like a “scattergun approach,” backing LIV Golf, planning an unlikely Winter Asian Games, bankrolling soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo, and buying the Premier League team Newcastle. All are varied approaches to “soft power.”

Ronaldo is reported to earn more than $200 million annually with Saudi club Al-Nassr.

Qatar's sovereign wealth fund controls French club Paris Saint-Germain, and Manchester City is controlled by an Abu Dhabi investment group. Ulrichsen argued sports teams are a more effective investment than World Cups or Olympics “because people care more about the teams they support than an event that happens for three or four weeks.”

“When Ronaldo would post on Instagram about the amazing lifestyle he was enjoying in Riyadh, that would reach upward of a half a billion people,” Ulrichsen added. “You simply can't buy that kind of reach with a conventional PR campaign.”

title: Rassie Erasmus set to miss 2027 Rugby World Cup group stage - Sports & Betting News
article_text:
Shockwaves have been sent across international rugby union, as World Rugby announce a six-game suspension for South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus.

The defending world champions fell to a rare defeat in Paris in round five of the 2026 Nations Championship leading to a bizarre rant from their head coach, accusing the referee and governing body of numerous wrongdoings.

In his post-match press conference on the Monday, which followed the defeat to France, Erasmus was as quoted saying "Is that not match fixing?! Is that not interfering with the outcome?" when referencing a number of so-called 'hip-drop' tackles which he believed were missed by the officials.

The ruling, which the back-to-back Rugby World Cup winners have already confirmed they have "requested a full hearing" to appeal, is set to have extreme ramifications for the Springboks and the whole of international rugby, with the showcase tournament just around the corner.

Should the suspension stand, the Springboks are set to be without their talismanic head coach - who has been in charge for both the 2019 and 2023 World Cup triumphs - for the start of the 2027 tournament.

On Tuesday evening, World Rugby announced that they had placed an automatic six-match suspension on South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus.

Two of those matches will be served in the remainder of the Autumn, with the other four set to be in 2027.

While South Africa's full 2027 Rugby World Cup warm up schedule may not have been released, as things stand, Rassie Erasmus would miss all three of South Africa's group stage matches.

Despite this, it is likely that the Springboks will confirm more World Cup warm-ups in due course, though it's unclear whether or not those would count towards Erasmus' suspension.

As things stand, Rassie Erasmus would return to the Springboks' hotseat for the Rugby World Cup round of 16, which gets underway on the weekend of the 23rd and 24th October 2027.

title: Scotland coach insists door remains open for Blyth-Lafferty to make World Cup
article_text:
The door remains open for Ollie Blyth-Lafferty to stake a claim for Scotland’s Rugby World Cup squad despite the young tighthead being omitted from the squad for the Nations Championship clash with Japan.

That is the view of assistant coach Pieter de Villiers, despite the Edinburgh youngster being released from the Scotland squad ahead of Saturday's game at Murrayfield.

Blyth-Lafferty was initially left out of Gregor Townsend’s squad for the autumn before being drafted in alongside his club-mate D’arcy Rae when Elliot Millar Mills was ruled out injured.

It was no surprise the 20-year-old was not thrown in against New Zealand or Australia but a game against a struggling Japan side presented an opportunity to test his ability at international level.

However, Scotland have decided to stick with established first choice Zander Fagerson plus Rae and Will Hurd for this weekend's game.

De Villiers, who won 69 caps as a tighthead prop in his own Test career, explained the decision to release Blyth-Lafferty, known as OBL, when he addressed the media on Tuesday afternoon.

"We're fortunate to have a good bit of tighthead depth at the moment," he said.

"When Elliot Millar Mills got injured, D’arcy Rae was the next tighthead in. But D’arcy was also just coming back from injury as well and we thought it was a brilliant opportunity for OBL as a young tighthead to come in as well and to just be with the group and grow with the group and measure himself against the international props as well.

"But D’arcy was always the next guy in. So as soon as he was 100 per cent fit to go, then normally we only keep three tightheads in the group.

"It was good to have OBL in and him getting exposure at club level often is good. Him training and scrummaging against the international props also gives him an idea to see where he is and where he still needs to grow as a young prop, which is only normal. So I think he's doing really well in his progress in becoming an international prop.

“But at the age of 20 as well, certain things will take a bit of time to settle and grow. So we're very happy with his progress, definitely.”

But the former France prop insisted the door remains open for Blyth-Lafferty to force his way into the picture next year ahead of the Rugby World Cup.

"There's definitely a chance for him," he said.

"He's done so well as a young tighthead to play professional club rugby and really scrummage well.

"The international level is a level up again and you also want to make sure that you put a young player in the best possible conditions for him to thrive. We tend to think that what we have done here in terms of exposing him is the best way. Getting more club rugby under the belt as well.

"This period from now onwards until the Six Nations will again be telling in terms of his growth and then we'll take it from there once the Six Nations come and we'll see how we go."

There have been comparisons made between Blyth-Lafferty and current first choice Zander Fagerson, who made his Scotland debut as 20-year-old a decade ago.

"He's done really well for us through this campaign," he said.

"As much as we've spoken about a couple of scrum frustrations that there were he's been consistent outside of set piece as well. He's been carrying well again.

"He's been training well. He's had a couple of niggles injury wise at the back end of last season which he's overcome. I think he's in great shape in terms of core conditioning and he's in great shape mentally as well.

"He's been strong for the group coming into this campaign and it's great to see him in great form."

title: ATP Finals: Alexander Zverev beats Ben Shelton to reach semi-finals
article_text:
World number one Alexander Zverev produced another serving masterclass against Ben Shelton to qualify for the ATP Finals knockout stage with a match to spare.

The German, 29, lost just two of the 31 points played on his serve in the second set as he completed an impressive 6-2 7-6 (7-4) win over fourth-ranked Shelton.

The two-time champion only made 10 unforced errors and landed 25 winners in a ruthless display to reach the semi-finals at the season-ending tournament for a fifth time.

The result confirmed Rafael Jodar's elimination, following the Spaniard's earlier 4-6 6-2 6-2 loss to French rising star Arthur Fils in the John McEnroe Group.

Zverev demonstrated the superb level which has taken him to the number one ranking and his first two Grand Slam titles in 2026.

He always appeared in control as he extended his unbeaten run against Shelton to seven matches - including victory in September's US Open final.

Having lost his first match as world number one at the Paris Masters in November, Zverev has backed up his status in Turin with two sweeping victories.

Just as in his victory over Jodar in his opening match, Zverev showed remarkable consistency on serve to starve the American of opportunities.

Shelton, who has risen to a career-high fourth in the world after winning four titles and reaching his first major final in 2026, managed to create just two break points in the match.

They came in the first set, when he already trailed by a break after Zverev struck in the opening game.

Shelton avoided falling a double break behind by twice saving a break point with an ace, but was quickly punished for his failure to take either of his chances in the following game as Zverev raced away with the set.

Zverev, who also won this year's French Open, maintained his grip on the match by winning each of the first 23 points on his serve in the second set.

Shelton managed to gain a foothold, and denied Zverev the chance to serve for the match by recovering from 15-40 down in the ninth game.

But, while the American reclaimed the first mini-break of the tie-break with a massive return, Zverev remained composed and fired in a wonderful on-the-run forehand winner to complete victory in stunning style.

With it, Zverev secured back-to-back wins against top-10 players for the first time since the 2024 ATP Finals before he faces Fils in the final group match.

Frenchman Fils claimed his first career win at the ATP Finals by battling to a comeback victory over Jodar which kept him in contention for a semi-final place.

In beating Jodar, 20, the 22-year-old Fils became the first Frenchman to record an ATP Finals victory since Jo-Wilfried Tsonga in 2011.

This was the youngest match by combined age at the season-ending tournament - which features the eight top-performing men - since a 21-year-old Novak Djokovic defeated a 20-year-old Juan Martin del Potro in 2008.

It was Fils, who has risen to a career-high ranking of seventh in the world during a season in which he triumphed at the ATP Masters 1000 in Cincinnati, who came out on top in a meeting between two of the men's game's most exciting rising stars.

Initially second-best as he struggled for rhythm - particularly on serve - in the opening set, Fils reset impressively to dominate sets two and three against an opponent who appeared to be fading physically.

A finalist at the Next Gen ATP Finals three years ago, Fils will fight for a place in the semi-finals against the already-qualified Zverev on Thursday, hoping to edge Shelton to a place in the knockout stage.

"It's going to be tough but I know that I can battle. I'm not afraid," said Fils of his showdown with Zverev, who plays Shelton later on Tuesday.

"It will be a nice match against the world number one. I don't have anything to lose, I'm just going to enjoy myself."

World number two Carlos Alcaraz plays Daniil Medvedev, while Flavio Cobolli meets Frances Tiafoe in the second round of Ivan Lendl Group matches on Wednesday.

In the men's doubles, Britain's Henry Patten and Finnish team-mate Harri Heliovaara fell to defeat in their second match.

The world number ones and defending champions won the first set but were beaten 6-7 (5-7) 6-3 10-4 by fourth seeds Marcelo Arevalo and Mate Pavic.

title: Report: Former LIV Golf star weighing shock one-year sabbatical after DP World Tour absence
article_text:
Former LIV Golf star Sebastian Munoz is reportedly considering taking a one-year break from professional golf, with the Colombian's future becoming an interesting talking point after missing out on a series of DP World Tour invites for 2027.

Munoz, 33, joined LIV Golf in 2023 and represented Joaquin Niemann's Torque GC throughout his time on the breakaway circuit. He enjoyed a significant moment in his LIV career last year, claiming his maiden individual victory at Indianapolis.

However, his name was notably absent from a group of nine former LIV players who have agreed to receive invitations to selected DP World Tour events next season. That absence does not necessarily mean Munoz was denied an opportunity, with it remaining unclear whether he was interested in pursuing the arrangement in the first place.

Nevertheless, Handicap 54 suggested on X that the Colombian could now be contemplating an extended absence from professional golf.

"The situation regarding the Colombian golfer Sebastián Muñoz is worth watching closely," posted Handicap 54, which is often among the first to break golf news across Latin America.

"It was notable that he was not included in the agreements with the DP World Tour, and it is my understanding that he has been considering taking a one-year sabbatical (this is not confirmed, but I know it is an option he has weighed)."

Munoz was not the only recognisable former LIV Golf player missing from the latest DP World Tour arrangements.

American veteran Charles Howell III was also notably absent, despite his name having previously been linked with a potential route onto the European circuit for the 2027 season.

His inclusion in those discussions had suggested that a move towards the DP World Tour could be an option, but that anticipated pathway has seemingly not materialised.

Howell had been representing Bryson DeChambeau's Crushers GC on LIV Golf. He won his sole LIV event at Mayakoba in 2023, and he won three times on the PGA Tour, with his first way back in 2002 and last in 2018.

The nine players who have agreed to receive DP World Tour invitations for the 2027 season include Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith, Bubba Watson, Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters.

Johnson, Watson and Smith are the most notable names, having collectively won five major titles between them, while Munoz's former Torque GC captain Niemann established himself as one of LIV Golf's most successful players, collecting nine individual titles and approximately $85.4 million in official prize money. Munoz's former Torque GC teammate Ancer also made the list.

Importantly, the agreements do not provide the nine players with full DP World Tour membership, unlike former LIV stars Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Patrick Reed, for example. Instead, they relate to invites for select tournaments, beginning with the Bapco Energies Bahrain Championship in January 2027.

The $10 million Rolex Series events are excluded, with designated tournaments identified for each player.

A separate group of nine former LIV players, including Sergio Garcia, Lee Westwood, Ian Poulter, Louis Oosthuizen and Martin Kaymer, also secured DP World Tour membership through the career money list.

Handicap 54 also used Munoz's situation to highlight wider concerns about the changing professional golf landscape and its potential impact on players from Latin America.

The account believes the end of PGA Tour Americas following the 2027 season, alongside concerns about the strength of Korn Ferry Tour fields, could leave important regional tournaments struggling to attract competitive players.

Those concerns come after the PGA Tour confirmed the final details of its new developmental structure, which will come into effect in 2028.

The Korn Ferry Tour will remain the principal pathway to the PGA Tour, while a new PGA Tour Challenger Series will provide another competitive tier.

The top 20 players on the Korn Ferry Tour will earn membership on the Challenger Series for the following season, while the top 90 players on the latter circuit will qualify for its season-ending championship.

PGA Tour Americas, meanwhile, will stage its final season in 2027 before being replaced by a network of affiliated events operated alongside third-party partners.

Although the PGA Tour believes the changes will create a more connected development system, Handicap 54 fears that players from Latin America could face greater financial and logistical obstacles when attempting to establish themselves professionally.

"The Latin American golf market appears to be collapsing, and no one seems to be doing anything to revive it," the account added.

A potential sabbatical would represent a significant development for a player who has previously established himself at the highest levels of both the PGA Tour and LIV Golf.

Before joining the breakaway league in 2023, Munoz claimed his only PGA Tour title at the 2019 Sanderson Farms Championship, defeating Sungjae Im in a playoff.

He subsequently represented the International Team at the 2022 Presidents Cup, collecting an impressive 2.5 points from three matches despite his side eventually losing 17.5-12.5 at Quail Hollow Club.

Munoz also earned a silver medal for Colombia at the 2023 Pan American Games, finishing just one stroke behind Mexico's Abraham Ancer, who was also a member of Torque GC.

For now, there has been no official confirmation that Munoz intends to step away from professional golf.

However, as Handicap 54's report suggests, with his future plans uncertain and the professional landscape continuing to evolve, the Colombian's next move will certainly be worth monitoring.

title: No regrets: Smylie outlines post-LIV Golf future
article_text:
Elvis Smylie has no regrets after leaving the LIV Golf building, as the Australian attempts to parlay a medical exemption into full-time European status.

- A rib injury forced the 2024 Australian PGA champion to the sidelines for almost three months after a $6 million solo win with LIV Golf.

- A medical exemption will give him key DP World Tour opportunities next year after LIV Golf announced it would wind down operations.

- Victory at next week's Australian PGA Championship or next month's Australian Open could fast-track his full-time status.

The 2024 Australian PGA champion was a $6 million solo winner on debut as part of Cameron Smith's all-Aussie LIV Golf team earlier this year.

However, as he balanced starts on both the rebel tour and Europe's DP World Tour, a rib injury became worse and eventually forced him onto the sidelines for almost three months.

The breakaway LIV Golf tour nosedived at the same time and announced this month it would begin winding down operations after losing key players and the funding needed to continue operating.

It left Smylie floundering for status and grinding in Spain's final round of European tour qualification, where he missed a spot despite shooting 22-under through six rounds.

However, ahead of this week's Queensland PGA Championship at Brisbane's Nudgee layout, the 24-year-old confirmed a medical exemption would offer him key opportunities next year.

"Eleven weeks out was hard to take and there were a lot of big tournaments I missed," he said.

"But the [DP World Tour] events I missed this year, I'll play next year, hopefully re-rank and get out there fulltime.

"It [LIV Golf] was great while it lasted and I took my opportunities.

"Financially it was great ... it meant I can have my team travel with me more often and with the injury, I learnt it's vital you have the right people around you.

"What I'm ready for is stability and consistency."

Smylie can fast-track his full-time status with victory at the Australian PGA Championship at The Lakes in Sydney next week, or at the Australian Open at Melbourne's Kingston Heath next month.

An Open victory also comes with a Masters invite, while a top-three finish earns a spot at the Open Championship.

Smith, Lucas Herbert and a host of LIV Golf's biggest names have also been granted various levels of access to the next European Tour season, bulking up an already quality field.

"It's going to make the tour better and the players are going to be working harder and harder," Smylie said.

Smylie will fancy his chances at Nudgee, where he was a Pennants-playing member as a child.

However, in his way is defending champion Cameron John, who punched his DP World Tour ticket with six rounds of 68 or better to finish third in Spain at 33-under.

title: Columbia University Publishes Economic Impact Study of the 2025 Ryder Cup
article_text:
Graduate students in Columbia University's Master of Science in Sports Management program have completed an independent economic impact study of the 2025 Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black, delivering their findings to 2025 Ryder Cup executive staff. The project was conducted as a supervised research course led by Brian Connolly, founder and managing principal of Victus Advisors, during the fall 2025 semester.

“The Ryder Cup’s influence extends far beyond the golf course. As golf’s premier team event, it brings thousands of attendees from around the world and generates meaningful economic impact for local communities, businesses and the broader region. Having Columbia University independently assess that impact provided tremendous value to the PGA of America. We were particularly impressed by the rigor of the students’ work and appreciated the opportunity to give the next generation of sports industry leaders a firsthand look at what it takes to plan and deliver a global sporting event. Their work also provided valuable insight into the Ryder Cup’s impact on the host community." - David Charles, Senior Director of Championships, PGA of America

“We are thrilled to have authored the economic impact report. This is yet another expression of the program's scholar-practitioner model that prepares our students with the practical skills needed to achieve success in the sports industry. Brian did a fantastic job leading our students through the process. We very much appreciate working with the PGA of America and their terrific staff, who allowed us the independence to conduct an analysis that yielded some amazing results for New York State.” - Scott Rosner, Program Director and Professor of Professional Practice, M.S. in Sports Management Program, Columbia University School of Professional Studies

“This project gave Columbia students a rare opportunity to contribute to a real-world analysis tied to one of the most legendary events in golf. I was impressed by the way they combined analytical rigor with practical problem-solving, especially given the scale and visibility of the Ryder Cup. The quality and defensibility of their economic impact analysis is a strong example of what the next generation of sports business professionals can bring to the industry.” - Brian Connolly, Lecturer, M.S. in Sports Management Program, Columbia University School of Professional Studies, Founder and Managing Principal, Victus Advisors

The Supervised Research Project is a course in Columbia's Master of Science in Sports Management program that places graduate students in a consulting role on an industry engagement. Most recently, at the behest of the PGA of America, the program produced an independent economic impact analysis of the 2025 Ryder Cup, held September 26-28, 2025, at Bethpage Black Golf Course in Farmingdale, New York.

Over the course of the semester, students worked through the full lifecycle of an economic and fiscal impact engagement, including client scoping and information requests, a site tour and kickoff meeting with the PGA of America, survey planning and distribution, and on-site event support at Bethpage Black. They then processed survey data, analyzed gross and net-new direct spending, estimated fiscal impacts, considered intangible benefits, provided a progress update to the client, prepared the final report, and presented their findings to PGA leadership.

The independent economic impact analysis conducted by Columbia University estimated that the 2025 Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black generated approximately $622.5 million in gross direct spending, including approximately $398.5 million in net new direct spending within New York State after accounting for displacement effects. The analysis combined ticket purchaser survey data (collected from 1,472 Ryder Cup attendees) with operational and event-related information, including ticket sales, hospitality, merchandise, sponsorship, staffing, taxes, attendee demographics, travel behavior and media reach. The findings showed substantial spending both at the event and across the broader visitor economy, including lodging, food and beverage, transportation and retail activity. Out-of-state visitors generated an estimated 193,946 hotel room nights, while total sales tax revenue to New York State was estimated at approximately $34.7 million. In addition to its direct economic and fiscal impacts, the study found that the Ryder Cup elevated New York’s global profile through significant tourism activity, international visitation, and media exposure.

Following her F1 ACADEMY title victory at the United States Grand Prix, Alisha will take to the track in Sin City with a bespoke golden championship livery, celebrating her title-winning season in style. The special-edition livery will make its debut at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit on Thursday 19 November, marking the final round of the 2026 season.

Commemorating her status as F1 ACADEMY Champion, every partner logo on the Red Bull Racing Academy Programme car and her No.21 will feature a golden chrome finish, set against an electric blue gradient backdrop inspired by Visa's signature colours. The design will be enhanced by a light-reactive metallic finish, creating a striking look fit for a champion under the bright lights of Las Vegas.

Alisha will also sport a special-edition race suit throughout the Grand Prix weekend, mirroring the electric blue gradient design that flows through her title-winning car.

Visa’s collaboration with Red Bull Racing Academy Programme pays tribute to Alisha’s achievement, whilst signifying the milestone behind it. The Team and Visa are proud to share the commitment of supporting emerging talent in their ambition to achieve success and inspire the next generation to pursue their own ambitions.

Alisha Palmowski, Red Bull Racing Academy Programme Driver, said: "I'm so excited to race in Las Vegas with this special championship livery! Visa and the Team have created something really special to celebrate my achievement, and I'm incredibly grateful to have that recognition on track for my final race in F1 ACADEMY. Although I've already secured the title, winning is always the goal, and it would be amazing to finish the season with a victory in this car!"

Caroline Buckland, Director of Marketing at Oracle Red Bull Racing, added: "Alisha has had an incredible season and has been a fantastic flagbearer for Red Bull Racing throughout her F1 ACADEMY career. We wanted to recognise her achievements and celebrate everything she's accomplished with a livery worthy of a champion. Alongside Visa, we're proud to give Alisha the opportunity to sign off her F1 ACADEMY career in style, with a car that reflects the success she's worked so hard to achieve.”

Andrea Fairchild, SVP, Global Sponsorship Strategy at Visa, said: “Alisha’s championship is an incredible achievement and a testament to her talent, ambition and determination. We’re proud to have supported her throughout this season and to celebrate this milestone with a livery that puts her accomplishment front and centre. Her journey represents the next generation of talent shaping the future of sport, and we’re proud to help create greater visibility for emerging athletes like Alisha as they take their next step.”
